title: You’ve got mail (finally): your Milburn cram sheet inside
gist: Resolution Foundation's weekly newsletter ahead of the Milburn Review: UK GDP grew 0.7% in Q3 but real household disposable income per person is flat; a roundup of evidence on youth hiring, mental health economics, work-search conditionality (Lone Parent Obligation lost ~90% of its savings) and remote work; plus a Chart of the Week arguing the UK's 20:1 benefits-to-employment-support spending ratio stems from low employment support, not high benefits.

insights.claim: UK GDP grew 0.7% in Q3, putting year-to-date growth second in the G7 behind only the US.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Headline UK growth momentum is stronger than expected, relevant for gilt and sterling outlook.
insights.quote: GDP grew 0.7 per cent in Q3, putting our year-to-date growth second in the G7, behind only the US

insights.claim: Real GDP per person in the UK has grown 2.6% over two years while real household disposable income per person has been essentially flat.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A divergence between output and household incomes points to weak consumer spending power and political pressure on living standards.
insights.quote: while real GDP per person has grown by 2.6% over the past two years, real household disposable income per person has been essentially flat

insights.claim: More than half of young UK jobseekers heard nothing back from any of their job applications in the last year.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Signals a weak entry-level labour market for young people.
insights.quote: more than half of young jobseekers heard nothing back from any of their job applications

insights.claim: A Reed survey of 2,000 UK firms found 73% say hiring early-career talent is a high priority, while citing gaps in understanding the working environment (34%), communication (33%) and reliability (32%), and 72% say scrapping employer NICs for under-25s would boost hiring.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Employer lobbying for under-25 NIC cuts is strong; Resolution Foundation views it as poor value, so watch policy outcome.
insights.quote: 72 per cent say scrapping employer NICs for under-25s would boost hiring

insights.claim: Stress, depression and anxiety accounted for 55% of UK working days lost to work-related ill health in 2024-25, and Danish research found people with depression, bipolar disorder or schizophrenia earn 31–73% less than their siblings.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Mental ill health is a major productivity and labour-supply cost, supporting demand for workplace mental-health interventions.
insights.quote: stress, depression and anxiety accounted for 55 per cent of UK working days lost to work-related ill health in 2024-25

insights.claim: A review argues rising mental health caseloads may not reflect worsening mental health, as UK survey distress among 16–19-year-olds rose only modestly since 2008, but Peter Fonagy's government review found the rise in common mental disorders among English adults (16% to 23% since 1993) cannot be explained by awareness alone.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: The diagnosis-vs-prevalence debate shapes how far welfare reform will target mental-health-related benefit claims.
insights.quote: “cannot be explained by greater awareness alone”

insights.claim: Economic shocks harm mental health: parental job loss in Brazil raised children's chance of a mental health diagnosis by 6 percentage points, while guaranteed legal representation for families facing eviction in New York cut new child mental health diagnoses by 7%.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Income and housing security have measurable health spillovers, relevant to welfare cuts' second-order fiscal costs.
insights.quote: In Brazil, parental job loss raised children’s chances of mental health diagnosis by 6 percentage points.

themes.theme: Conditionality's hidden costs: Lone Parent Obligation

insights.claim: IFS research on the Lone Parent Obligation, which cut the youngest-child age for single-parent work search from 16 to five between 2008 and 2012, found employment rose 4.4 percentage points but typical jobs paid only £8,000 a year.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Conditionality raises employment but into low-paid work with little tax yield.
insights.quote: Employment rose by 4.4 percentage points – although the typical job paid just £8,000 a year, yielding little tax.

insights.claim: Almost 90% of the gross saving from the Lone Parent Obligation disappeared through higher disability benefit claims and lower future tax payments, and among children already struggling at school GCSE results fell and absence rose.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Warns that 'tough love' benefit cuts in the Milburn agenda may deliver far smaller fiscal savings than scored.
insights.quote: Almost 90 per cent of the gross saving disappeared

themes.theme: Remote work as an employment lever

insights.claim: Using the pandemic jump in UK home working as a natural experiment, each one-point rise in home working lifted full-time employment by nearly 1% for disabled workers and 0.4% for 50–64-year-olds, explaining roughly three-quarters of the rise in full-time disabled employment.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Rolling back remote work could undermine labour-supply gains among older and disabled workers; relevant to return-to-office policy debates.
insights.quote: Home working explained roughly three-quarters of the rise in full-time disabled employment.

themes.theme: Milburn Review cheat sheet: levy, subsidies and benefits

insights.claim: Since 2019/20, 57% of levy-funded apprenticeship starts in England have been for adults aged 25 and over, and this group accounts for all growth in levy-funded starts since 2022/23.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Supports the case for ringfencing the levy for young people, a potential hit to adult/higher-level training providers.
insights.quote: this group accounting for all the growth in levy-funded starts since 2022/23

insights.claim: Removing National Insurance for under-25s would cost £132,000 per additional young person in work versus £36,000 for boosting employment subsidy schemes.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Targeted subsidies are about 3.7x more cost-effective, favouring them over tax cuts in Milburn recommendations.
insights.quote: the first would cost £132,000 for every additional young person in work while the second £36,000

insights.claim: 260,000 young people receive Universal Credit Health with no requirements or support, and for 120,000 young people Universal Credit Health and/or PIP is the difference between being in poverty or not.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Benefit cuts for young claimants carry direct poverty risks, constraining the scope of reform.

insights.claim: Alan Milburn says that for every £1 spent on employment support for young people, £25 is spent on their benefits, and his review is expected to shift that balance by both cutting benefits and increasing employment support.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Anticipate a reform package combining benefit cuts with expanded employment support spending.
insights.quote: for every £1 spent on employment support (training, job search help, wage subsidies) for young people, £25 is spent on their benefits
insights.locator: Alan Milburn wants you to know

insights.claim: Across OECD countries (all ages), the UK spends about twenty times as much on benefits as on employment support, versus a five-to-one ratio exceeded by only a handful of countries including Sweden, Denmark and Korea, and the high UK ratio is caused by low employment support spending rather than high benefit spending.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Undercuts the narrative of an overly generous UK benefit system; the fix is spending more on activation, not just cutting benefits.
insights.quote: It is low employment support spending, rather than high benefit spending, that is causing our high ratio.
